name: Gadusol
lead: Gadusol is a small natural UV-absorbing compound (C8H12O6), a substituted cyclohexenone, found in the eggs of fish and in some other vertebrates and invertebrates.[1] It was isolated from cod roe, where it occurs at about 4 g per kg dry weight, and its structure was confirmed by synthesis in 1981.[3] It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids that organisms in high-sunlight environments use as natural sunscreens.[1]

For appearance, the interest is as a bio-derived sunscreen filter: UV exposure drives sunburn, tanning, photoageing and skin damage, and a compound that absorbs UV while also acting as an antioxidant could help protect skin tone and keep the complexion looking younger.[4][14] Researchers have proposed gadusol for sunscreens and cosmetics, and a 2019 paper framed novel microbe-made sunscreens as an alternative to filters such as oxybenzone and octinoxate, which have been reported to be toxic to juvenile coral.[4][11][7]

Gadusol is not an established commercial cosmetic ingredient. The research base spans isolation chemistry, photophysics, computational modelling, vertebrate biology, engineered yeast and bacterial production, and one in vivo human skin spectroscopy study of gels containing gadusol.[3][5][6][7][12][13]

paras: A 1981 study isolated gadusol from cod ovaries just before spawning, identified it as 1,4,5-trihydroxy-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methoxycyclohex-1-en-3-one, confirmed the structure by synthesis, and found similar concentrations in the roes of other marine teleosts.[3] It was long assumed that fish obtained such compounds from diet or symbionts. A 2015 eLife paper reported that fish can synthesise gadusol de novo and that analogous pathways are present in amphibians, reptiles and birds; the authors also showed engineered yeast carrying the fish genes can produce and secrete gadusol, and suggested this as a route to large-scale production for pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.[7]

Wikipedia lists gadusol as produced by marine vertebrates and invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles and birds.[1] A 2023 Current Biology study using gadusol-deficient mutant zebrafish found that maternally provided gadusol is the primary sunscreen in embryonic and larval fish, protecting them from UV-induced DNA damage; in vertebrates melanin had been the only sunscreen known, and it often appears late in embryonic development.[12][15]

Gadusol absorbs UV through its conjugated ring, which Wikipedia says helps protect biomolecules from damage.[1] Computational work using high-level quantum chemistry assessed the structural features behind its photoprotective capacity, including how the enol-enolate equilibrium influences photophysical properties.[8] A photophysics study examined its excited-state behaviour and reductive quenching,[9] and antioxidant activity has been measured in extracts of fish roes from the Argentine Sea.[10]

A 2020 photochemistry study measured how efficiently gadusol species quench singlet oxygen. Gadusolate, the main species at biological pH, was a more efficient quencher than the enol form, and the authors concluded that its role as a sacrificial antioxidant should be considered alongside its UV-screening function in biotechnological applications.[14]

A 2020 review of marine cosmetics identifies mycosporine-like amino acids and gadusol as important lines of enquiry in topical photoprotection.[4] A 2019 ACS Synthetic Biology paper described an engineered pathway combining genes from a vertebrate and two Gram-positive bacteria to form novel sunscreen compounds with hybrid structures, motivated by the search for filters less harmful to coral than oxybenzone and octinoxate.[11] Wikipedia also cites a 2023 study comparing gadusol with the synthetic UV filter benzophenone-3.[1]

No clinical trials of gadusol as a sunscreen or skin treatment have been found. One published in vivo human study used confocal Raman spectroscopy to examine the depth profile and photoprotective effects of Pluronic F127 gels containing mycosporine-like amino acids and gadusol on human skin, analysing biochemical changes under UV radiation.[13] Other work is laboratory, computational and animal research, including the zebrafish embryo studies.[12][8][9]

card.summary: Natural fish-roe UV absorber studied as a bio-derived sunscreen molecule; lab and computational work only, no human trials.
card.note: Not an established cosmetic ingredient; no human studies found.

quick.overview:
Gadusol is a small molecule that fish eggs and some other animals carry to absorb sunlight. It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids made by algae and corals.

Researchers have proposed it as a natural sunscreen ingredient and have engineered microbes to produce it.
quick.mechanism: Its conjugated ring structure absorbs UV radiation, and it also has antioxidant activity measured in fish-roe extracts.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy studies were found. It is not an established commercial sunscreen filter.

chain: Gadusol absorbs UV through its conjugated ring
UV damage and oxidative stress in skin are reduced
Skin tone and texture stay protected from sun-driven ageing
angle.text: Gadusol is being explored as a natural UV filter and antioxidant for sun-care products, where the appearance goal is less sun damage and photoageing. It is a research-stage ingredient rather than a product people buy today.
